title: 道德經 第二十一章
source: Laozi 老子, 道德經 (Daodejing), chapter 21, in the Wang Bi 王弼 recension (華亭張氏原本, 晉 王弼注), as transcribed at Chinese Wikisource; verified character-for-character against the printed public-domain edition of Paul Carus, Lao-Tze's Tao-Teh-King: Chinese-English (Chicago: Open Court, 1898), p. 63. All punctuation is editorial — the original has none — and the division into 81 chapters is traditional. Sense-units follow Wang Bi's own commentary lemmata. Translations are made fresh from the Chinese. Pronunciation convention: modern Mandarin, given in Hanyu Pinyin — an admitted anachronism, and the living convention for reading these texts. Where an Old Chinese rhyme is invisible in Mandarin, a note says so. Prepared audio is synthesized speech in that same convention (cmn-CN-Chirp3-HD-Achernar).
about: Chapter 21 of the Daodejing. Its traditional title is 虛心 (Emptying the Heart). The chapter titles are not part of the text and are not Wang Bi's: they come from the Heshanggong 河上公 recension and are carried here only as navigation labels, so a chapter can be found by something other than its number. The received text is Wang Bi's (3rd c. AD); the manuscripts found at Mawangdui (1973) and Guodian (1993) are older and differ in places, and the notes flag those differences where they matter. Classical Chinese has no inflection, no obligatory subject, and no fixed parts of speech — the notes show how the line produces its meaning. Read the characters; the pinyin under each one is a reading aid you can hide with the transcription button.

sentences.t:
孔德之容，
惟道是從。

morph.gloss: hollow, empty — Wang Bi glosses the character outright as 空 kōng, and the English here follows him; standing on its own 孔 is 'vast, great'
potency — the power a thing has by simply being what it is
bearing, the way a thing carries and holds itself
only, solely — the same word as 唯 in chapter 15's 夫唯
the Way — and here the OBJECT of the verb at the end, pulled to the front
not 'is': a pronoun standing in for the object that has just been moved ahead of its verb
to follow, to go along after

sentences.l:
The bearing of hollow potency —
it is the Way alone that it follows.
sentences.i: Potency that is hollow carries itself in one way only: it follows the Way and nothing else.
sentences.n: 惟道是從 is a construction worth learning whole. Classical Chinese normally puts the object after the verb, but to single an object out it moves the object in front and leaves 是 behind it as a placeholder: 惟 X 是 V, 'it is X and X alone that is V-ed'. So this is not 'only the Way is followed' with 是 as a verb 'to be' — the language has no such verb, as chapter 1 said. 孔 is disputed. Heshanggong glosses it 大 'great', which gives 'the bearing of the great potency'; Wang Bi, our first authority, glosses it 空 'empty' and says that only by taking emptiness as one's potency can one move in step with the Way. We follow Wang Bi, as the house rule requires, and record the other reading here. 容 you met in chapter 15 (強為之容, 'forcing a description of it') and chapter 16 (知常容, 'roomy'); the character covers both what a thing looks like and how much it can hold.

sentences.t:
道之為物，
惟恍惟惚。

morph.gloss: the subject-to-predicate particle: it turns 'the Way is a thing' into 'the Way's being a thing'
to be, to count as (wéi; wèi would be 'for the sake of')
a thing, an object among objects
a glimmer, dim — showing at the edge of sight and gone
a blur, not to be made out

sentences.l:
The Way's being a thing —
only a glimmer, only a blur.
sentences.i: Take the Way as a thing, and it is nothing but glimmer and blur.
sentences.n: 之 doing its third job again — sitting between a subject and what is said of it, and making the whole into a phrase, exactly as 冰之將釋 did in chapter 15. Chapter 14 christened 惚恍 as one word, 'the blur'; here the two halves come apart and are handed a 惟 each.

sentences.t:
惚兮恍兮，
其中有象；
恍兮惚兮，
其中有物。

morph.gloss: (the sighing particle of southern song — breath, not meaning)
the middle, what is held inside (zhōng; read zhòng it is 'to hit the mark')
an image — a shape seen, not a thing handled

sentences.l:
Blurred! — dim! —
and within it there are images;
dim! — blurred! —
and within it there are things.
sentences.i: A blur, a glimmer — and inside it, shapes; a glimmer, a blur — and inside it, things.
sentences.n: The two couplets say the same two words in opposite order, and then move from 象 to 物: from the image of a thing to the thing itself. That is the direction of the whole chapter — it starts at the far edge of the visible and works inward, image, thing, essence, proof. 象 is the character chapter 14 used for 無物之象, 'the image of no-thing'; it is what you see when there is nothing to touch.

sentences.t:
窈兮冥兮，
其中有精；

morph.gloss: deep down and out of sight, as at the bottom of a well
unlit, black — the dark of a place no light reaches
the finest stuff in a thing — its concentrated life, what is left when everything coarse is sifted out

sentences.l:
Deep! — dark! —
and within it there is essence;
sentences.i: Far down, unlit — and inside it, the essence of the thing;
sentences.n: 精 is grain hulled clean — the character is 米 'rice' beside a phonetic — and from that, the refined part of anything. Later Daoist writing narrows it to a fluid the body stores, and a reading that makes it 'seed' here is reading that back in; at this date it is simply what is most concentratedly real in a thing.

sentences.t:
其精甚真，
其中有信。

morph.gloss: real, genuine — the true thing and not a counterfeit of it
what bears a thing out — a token, a proof that it is so

sentences.l:
Its essence utterly real;
within it there is what bears witness.
sentences.i: That essence is wholly real, and inside it lies what makes good on it.
sentences.n: 其精甚真 has no verb at all — 'its essence / very / real' — and English cannot say it without supplying 'is'. 信 is the same character that means good faith in chapter 17, and it comes back in that sense two chapters on, at the end of chapter 23; Wang Bi glosses it here 信驗, 'proof, what verifies', so it is the evidence a thing gives of itself rather than the trust anyone places in it. One word covering both is not sloppiness: to the language they are the same thing seen from the two ends.

sentences.t:
自今及古，
其名不去，

morph.gloss: from — here the preposition, NOT the reflexive 'self' of 自然
to depart, to go away — the classical sense, the reverse of modern Mandarin 'to go to'

sentences.l:
From now reaching back to antiquity,
its name does not depart,
sentences.i: From today back to the beginning of things, its name has never fallen away,
sentences.n: Two things here. 自 is the reflexive 'self' everywhere else in this book — 自然, 自見, 自是 — but in front of a word for time or place it is the plain preposition 'from'. And the direction is backwards: from now to antiquity, where you would expect 自古及今, 'from antiquity to now', which is what many editions print. Two things speak for the order printed here. It rhymes: 古 gǔ, 去 qù and 甫 fǔ end three lines running and all three belong to one Old Chinese rhyme group — a rhyme Mandarin has kept, so you can hear the argument for yourself, and reversing the phrase loses it. And the Mawangdui silk manuscripts read 自今及古 too; it is the Heshanggong line of texts that has 自古及今.

morph.gloss: by it, thereby — the preposition with its object left out, as so often
to pass in review, to look over one by one, as a commander does his troops
the beginnings of them all — where every thing started
a beginning — the sense Wang Bi gives the character here; on its own it is 'just now', or the polite name a man took at his capping

sentences.l: thereby to review the beginnings of them all.
sentences.i: and by it we survey how everything began.
sentences.n: 眾甫 is bound into one tap-unit because 甫 does not mean 'beginning' on its own: it is a polite name given to a grown man, or the adverb 'just now'. Wang Bi glosses the pair outright — 眾甫，物之始也, 'the 眾甫 are the beginnings of things' — and a gloss on either half alone would have to explain the pair anyway, which is the sign that it should be learned whole. Some readers keep the ordinary sense and translate 'the fathers of the multitude', i.e. the ancestors; the two readings come out close, since what fathers a thing is where it begins.

sentences.t:
吾何以知眾甫之狀哉？
以此。

morph.gloss: by what? — the question word stands in front of the preposition it belongs to
a beginning — the sense Wang Bi gives the character here; on its own it is 'just now', or the polite name a man took at his capping
the look of a thing, the shape it presents
(the final particle that closes a question — here a real one, and the two characters after it are the answer)

sentences.l:
By what do I know the look of the beginnings of them all?
By this.
sentences.i: How do I know what the beginnings of everything look like? By this.
sentences.n: 何以 is 以何 with the question word dragged to the front — the fixed rule you met in chapter 13's 何謂寵辱若驚: an interrogative pronoun goes before the word that governs it, never after. 'By this' — by what? The text does not say, and Wang Bi takes it as by what has just been described: the glimmer, the blur, and the essence found inside them. The chapter ends by pointing rather than explaining, and the same closing formula returns later in the book.
